source: Alexander, P. 2010. 'Large Ruminant Reproduction Workshop', ACIAR AH 2005/086, presented in Cambodia (mekonglivestock.wordpress.com). Only the practically farmer-relevant sections are extracted here; the source also covers advanced reproductive technologies (AI, embryo transfer, cloning) that are academic/veterinary-training content rather than farmer-facing and were excluded from this batch.
text: Correctly spotting when a cow or buffalo is in heat (oestrus) is described in three stages. Coming on: sniffing or attempting to mount other animals, increased restlessness, frequent urination, and a moist, enlarged vulva, with other cows showing interest but not yet standing still to be mounted. On (standing heat): the defining sign is the female standing still to be mounted; other signs include attempting to mount others herself, frequent bellowing, reduced milk yield if lactating, and visible evidence of having been mounted (tail rubs, mud on the flanks). Going off: no longer standing to be ridden, continued smelling/nudging activity, and dried mucous discharge around the perineum. Standing heat itself lasts about 15 hours on average (range roughly 2-30 hours), and the full oestrus cycle length is 18-24 days in a normal healthy cow. The source also notes buffalo signs are more subtle and harder to detect than in cattle, and that buffalo reach first oestrus later (24-36 months vs. 7-18 months in cattle) and have a longer gestation (300-340 days vs. around 285 days in cattle).
